rounds.hypothesis: Round 1, from diagnose: the sigevent dispatch in sys_timer_create has SIGEV_THREAD as a bare `unimplemented!()`. SIGEV_THREAD = 2 is a value `SigNotify::try_from` accepts, so the arm is reachable with well-formed input from any unprivileged process, and the Rust panic becomes a kernel halt (PANIC_ON_OOPS), discarding every LTP result from that boot. Linux's good_sigevent() treats SIGEV_THREAD identically to SIGEV_SIGNAL -- validate sigev_signo, target the thread group -- because creating the thread that runs sigev_un._sigev_thread.function is the C library's job. The same no-panic rule should hold for the sibling arms in create_timer that the second caller (sys_timerfd_create) can reach.
rounds.change: Merged SIGEV_THREAD into the SIGEV_SIGNAL arm as `SigNotify::SIGEV_SIGNAL | SigNotify::SIGEV_THREAD`, replacing the stale TODO with a comment on why the kernel owes nothing more. Range-checked sigev_signo with `u8::try_from` before narrowing (replacing `SigNum::try_from(signo as u8)`) in both signal-delivering arms. Replaced the three `unimplemented!()` arms in create_timer (Pid/Tid dynamic scheduling clock, Fd clock) with EINVAL. Uncommented timer_create01 in all.txt.
rounds.outcome: Selector run printed `All conformance tests passed.` kirk reported passed 25 / skipped 15 / failed 0 / broken 0 / warnings 0 under RELEASE=1. Lints clean.

rounds.hypothesis: Round 2, after verify returned `regressed` (9 TPASS, early exit during the SIGEV_SIGNAL iteration at CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID, never reaching SIGEV_THREAD). My first explanation -- 'a helper function compiled differently in debug' -- was not a root cause, and inlining it did not fix anything; verify saw the same 9. Discarded it. New hypothesis from the shape of the failure: the kernel is delivering all 25 results and the loss is in how the result is captured or counted, not in the syscall. Rival hypotheses to kill: a signal firing when none should (the test never arms a timer), a CPU-time-clock path that blocks, and timing sensitivity under a slower build.
rounds.change: No kernel change this round. Instrumented with a scratch edit to run_ltp_test.sh (since reverted, never committed) to (a) run the test binary directly and unbuffered to the console, bypassing kirk and the buffered $LOG_FILE, (b) run it through a pipe, into a file, and pipe-to-file to test the kernel's output path, and (c) dump kirk's per-test JSON alongside direct-run ground truth for two already-enabled control tests. Also read Timer::new/add_posix_timer to settle the spurious-firing hypothesis, and libkirk/ltp.py to find the counting rule.
rounds.outcome: Root-caused, and it is not a kernel defect. In one debug boot on the same kernel: a direct run of timer_create01 gives passed 25 / skipped 15 across all 5 notify types including SIGEV_THREAD, exit 0, while kirk in that same boot reports 9. Kernel output path exonerated -- console, pipe, file, and pipe-to-file all yield 25 TPASS and the full 3658 bytes. Spurious firing ruled out by code: Timer::new starts from TimerInner::default() with an empty timer_callback, and add_posix_timer only stores the Arc, so no TimerCallback is inserted until set_timeout; a freshly created timer cannot fire. The counting rule is in libkirk/ltp.py read_result: it first tries _SUMMARY_RE against LTP's `Summary:` block and only if that fails falls back to `stdout.count('TPASS')` with `skipped = stdout.count('TSKIP')`. Truncated capture loses the Summary block, so the fallback runs, and skipped reads 0 because LTP emits TCONF, not TSKIP -- exactly the 9/0 signature. Proven pre-existing with a control, one debug boot, direct-run truth vs kirk: chmod01 32 TPASS / 2140 bytes -> kirk 32 (correct); confstr01 34 TPASS / 2817 bytes -> kirk 14 (truncated); timer_create01 25 TPASS / 3658 bytes -> kirk 9 (truncated). confstr01 is an already-enabled test that runs in CI today and has nothing to do with timers, so this is a pre-existing kirk capture limit around 2 KB, not a regression from this fix. Final debug run of the shipping patch: failed 0 / broken 0 / warnings 0, `All conformance tests passed.`, make exit 0. Lints clean: format_all --check, clippy_check workspace (exit 0, zero warnings), typos.

layer: As diagnosed: the syscall entry layer -- the sigevent interpretation in sys_timer_create plus the create_timer helper beside it in kernel/src/syscall/timer_create.rs. This is where sigev_notify and sigev_signo are validated and turned into an expiry action, and it is the layer that owes userspace an errno rather than an oops. Asterinas has no posix-timer core between the syscall and the per-clock TimerManager, so this function is the closest equivalent to Linux's good_sigevent placement. I patched create_timer's dynamic-clock arms as well because owning_layer named them as part of the same invariant and other_callers named sys_timerfd_create as reaching them -- a widening within the diagnosed layer, not a disagreement with it.
generalizes: Nothing branches on a flag, size, or errno the test happens to use. (a) SIGEV_THREAD is not special-cased -- its arm is deleted and merged into SIGEV_SIGNAL, so the two notify types cannot drift apart, and every sigev_signo behaves the same for both: 1..=64 accepted, 0 / 65 / negative / >255 rejected with EINVAL. The test only ever passes SIGALRM, so correctness for the other 63 signal numbers comes from sharing the arm, not from the test. sys_timer_create is the only caller that parses a sigevent, so there is no other caller of this arm to break. glibc users are unaffected either way, because glibc rewrites SIGEV_THREAD into a SIGEV_THREAD_ID aimed at its own helper thread and never passes SIGEV_THREAD to the kernel; this fixes the raw-syscall path that LTP and Go-style runtimes use. (b) The sigev_signo range check fixes inputs the test never supplies: sigev_signo=257 previously truncated to 1 and was wrongly accepted, and now returns EINVAL as Linux does. It applies to SIGEV_THREAD_ID too, an arm the test walks only with a valid signo, so it is strictly a widening of validation rather than anything the test observes. It also moves the still-blocked timer_create02 toward passing, since its `wrong sigev_signo` case passes INT_MAX. (c) The create_timer EINVAL arms fix the second caller named in other_callers: sys_timerfd_create forwards clockid without validation, so a negative clockid decoding to a SCHED or FD dynamic clock used to halt the kernel from either syscall and now returns an errno. No caller could have depended on the old behaviour, because the old behaviour was a panic. Deliberately left alone: the same-shaped `unimplemented!()` in read_clock (kernel/src/syscall/clock_gettime.rs) belongs to sys_clock_gettime's dispatch rather than this layer, and the `sig_num as u8` truncations in kill.rs, pidfd_send_signal.rs and prctl.rs belong to their own syscalls' validation. Both are the same defect class and worth separate commits; folding them in here would be scope creep across syscall boundaries.
fix_summary: sys_timer_create no longer panics on valid userspace input. SIGEV_THREAD is served by enqueueing sigev_signo to the calling process's thread group, exactly as SIGEV_SIGNAL is, because spawning the thread that runs sigev_un._sigev_thread.function is the C library's job and not the kernel's; sigev_signo is range-checked in 1..=SIGRTMAX before being narrowed to a SigNum; and the dynamic scheduling-clock and FD-clock paths in create_timer return EINVAL instead of halting the kernel. Designed against Asterinas's own abstractions rather than Linux's structure: Linux factors sigevent checking into a separate good_sigevent() that returns a struct pid for the timer core to target later, but Asterinas has no posix-timer core -- sys_timer_create builds a boxed `dyn Fn()` expiry closure submitted as a WorkItem, and the natural way to express `target the thread group` is to clone the Arc<Process> into that closure and call Process::enqueue_signal(KernelSignal). Since the SIGEV_SIGNAL arm already builds exactly that closure, expressing `SIGEV_THREAD behaves as SIGEV_SIGNAL` becomes a match-arm merge rather than a new validation layer -- both smaller and harder to let drift than porting good_sigevent's shape. SigNum::try_from remains the single source of truth for the 1..=64 bound.
caveat: The number verify reads for this test is understated by the harness, and that is worth knowing before this is measured again. In a debug build kirk reports 9 passed / 0 skipped for timer_create01, while the test itself reports passed 25 / skipped 15 in the same boot. The cause is in libkirk/ltp.py read_result, not in the kernel: kirk's captured stdout is truncated somewhere above ~2 KB, which loses LTP's `Summary:` block, so kirk falls back to `stdout.count('TPASS')` and reports skipped=0 because it counts TSKIP while LTP emits TCONF. It is pre-existing and unrelated to this fix -- in the same debug boot, the already-enabled confstr01 (34 TPASS, 2817 bytes) is likewise reported as 14, while the smaller chmod01 (32 TPASS, 2140 bytes) is reported correctly as 32. It is a reporting-fidelity bug and not a pass/fail one: failed/broken/warnings stay 0, the per-test status stays `pass`, and the gate prints `All conformance tests passed.` in both debug and release. Worth its own run against kirk's capture path; treating the low count as a kernel regression would be chasing the wrong layer.
